items.title: OI-AADX: an optimised image-based Android Adware detection using eXplainable AI
items.abstract: Existing Machine learning (ML)/Deep Learning (DL) based android malware detection approaches suffer from a series of issues viz. Adversarial Robustness, Higher Computational Complexity, Data Scarcity and Imbalance, Explainability and Interpretation, Higher False Positives and Meta/Polymorphic Nature of Malware. Our focus in this research is on two aspects viz. (a) addressing the Explainability and Interpretation issue that typically the DL-based techniques suffer from and (b) optimisation. In this paper, we propose a CNN-based adware detection method that uses an Android permission-based dataset (MadDroid). We convert the dataset permissions into black and white images and use them to train the proposed CNN model. We use eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to get SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and use them to find the feature’s contribution in the prediction of our model. By following this, the number of features reduces from 440 to 144 key features. We apply statistical methods to analyse SHAP values and highlight the most significant features by training and testing our model on each reduced dataset. We systematically find out the important features using CNN and XAI, and we have maintained the sequence of permission in the image to maintain the same sequence as the original feature set.

items.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the \textbf{training-inference mismatch} between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. \textit{We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.} Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a \textit{numerical discrepancy} of the engine and a \textit{policy lag} of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the \textbf{discrepancy-lag correction} (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.

items.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
items.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.

items.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
items.abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

items.title: ONVERSATIONAL AI FOR MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT
items.abstract: Mental health support remains difficult to access for many individuals because of cost, stigma, limited availability of professionals, geographical barriers, and hesitation in discussing personal concerns.Conversational Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly systems based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs), offers a potential supplementary channel through which users can communicate in natural language and receive basic emotional or informational support.However, mental health is a sensitive application area in which fluent responses alone are not sufficient: reliability, contextual understanding, empathy, privacy, safety, bias, emotional dependency, and appropriate referral to human professionals are important concerns.This paper reviews the development and application of conversational AI for mental health support and synthesizes the gaps identified in the reviewed literature.Based on these gaps, a conceptual framework is proposed that combines user-input analysis, conversational context, LLM-based response generation, safety validation, and supportive response or professional referral.The framework is evaluated conceptually using eight dimensions: response relevance, empathy, context awareness, reliability, safety, privacy, usability, and transparency.The paper emphasizes that conversational AI should function as a supportive technological tool rather than a replacement for qualified mental health professionals.

items.title: Open tools for the authentic assessment of GenAI-assisted practices
items.abstract: Learning can be viewed as a process of enculturation that involves coming to understand how to use culturally relevant tools. It follows that, if we want to make valid assessments of and for learning, we need to account for how students use those tools. Traditional assessment practices tend to privilege tools in the head over tools in the world. But simply allowing students access to external tools like generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) during assessments is not sufficient to ensure validity. Hutchins’ work suggests that open tools—those that make problem steps and solutions more visible—provide wide horizons of observation and, in turn, provide evidence that can be used to make and justify assessment claims. Learning analytics platforms are one way to open up tools and widen horizons. However, current versions break the connection between tools and the cultures they represent, pulling interactions out of their authentic context of use. This chapter proposes a potential solution: we can instrument authentic tools in ways that widen our horizon of observation and move us towards more authentic assessment of GenAI-assisted practices.

items.title: Opening the Box Changes the Cat: LLMs Detect Chain-of-Thought Monitoring - What now?
items.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning allows large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate reasoning traces in natural language while solving complex tasks. These traces can support safety monitoring by exposing potentially harmful plans before actions are executed. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which LLMs infer the presence of CoT monitoring from direct and indirect environmental cues and examine how this inference affects their subsequent behavior. Our observations suggest that oversight is an interactive process: while a monitor inspects a model's reasoning, traces left by monitoring interventions can allow the model to infer that its thoughts are being observed and to adapt its behavior accordingly. We show that even subtle environmental cues, such as timing-related signals from timeouts and operation durations, can reveal the presence of monitoring and trigger models to adapt their behavior. Across repeated episodes and interaction loops, we further observe that models can form statistical estimates of the monitor's effectiveness and use these estimates to guide attempts to evade detection. These findings highlight the need to evaluate CoT-based oversight under adaptive conditions, where the monitoring process itself may influence the behavior it seeks to observe.

items.title: Operational Security in CRDT-Based Collaborative Editing Systems
items.abstract: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) enable real-time collaborative editing by allowing distributed participants to modify local copies of shared documents while ensuring eventual convergence. Although this architecture provides availability and synchronization benefits, it introduces significant operational security challenges when participants cannot be fully trusted. This presentation examines security limitations in CRDT-based collaborative editing systems, focusing on Yjs, Automerge, Loro, and associated synchronization infrastructures. Particular attention is given to the persistence of deleted sensitive information, document-level authorization constraints, client identity impersonation, synchronization failures caused by rejected operations, the potential loss of offline contributions, and limitations of participant revocation. The analysis incorporates technical demonstrations and reproducible experiments involving Yjs, Hocuspocus, y-websocket, and Durable Streams. These examples illustrate how malicious participants may manipulate operation identifiers, impersonate legitimate collaborators, and compromise the integrity of shared documents. A central contribution is the examination of artificial intelligence agents as active CRDT participants. The presentation demonstrates how AI-assisted editing can amplify existing authorization weaknesses through confused-deputy scenarios, excessive agency, and exposure to untrusted document content. It further discusses the implications of the Agents Rule of Two for collaborative AI systems. Practical security recommendations include separating untrusted content from editing privileges, introducing human review before applying AI-generated modifications, restricting agent capabilities through dedicated tools, assigning distinct agent identities, and implementing cryptographically verifiable operations. Fine-grained access control at the document-section level is also considered as a direction for improving collaborative editing security. The presentation highlights the need to integrate access control, identity verification, cryptographic integrity, and human oversight into the architecture of secure CRDT-based collaborative systems.

items.title: Operationalising human–AI interaction requirements through DigComp 3.0 for translator education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing the landscape of translation, expanding translators’ involvement in interaction configurations, evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and governance of risks within augmented translation environments. This study defines Human–AI Interaction in Translation (HAIT) as GenAI-mediated component of the human-centred augmented translation process, where GenAI is integrated into translation technologies and conversational large language models. Translation education lacks a developmental structure that connects these emerging requirements and their related digital competences to curriculum design. This study proposes a workflow-derived operationalisation of HAIT for translator education. A conceptual functional analysis of augmented translation workflows produced eight HAIT requirements, which were mapped to the 21 competences of the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp 3.0) by assessing 168 potential relationships for functional correspondence, scope fidelity, and traceable justification. The analysis accepted 37 relationships among 16 competences and identified translation-specific residues that require curricular supplementation. The operationalised requirements were organised into a proposed four-level progression informed by DigComp proficiency levels. An exploratory mixed-methods pilot with 42 second-year translation students examined perceived relevance after contextualised exposure in a course-embedded intervention. Students broadly perceived DigComp as relevant to translation education and practice, particularly focusing on competences related to familiar topics such as privacy protection, device security, copyright, information retrieval, communication and collaboration, with limited attention to information evaluation and programming competences. Their responses were less explicit about AI-generated output evaluation, prompting and in-context steering, grounding configuration, and risk-responsive actions, highlighting the value of a spiral curriculum for competence development and Quality Education (SDG4).

items.title: Optimization Techniques for Solving the Minimum Red--Blue Separating Set Problem with an Application to Human--AI Text Separation
items.abstract: We study the so-called Minimum Red''Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) which arises from computational geometry. In particular, we propose a compact Set-Cover ILP formulation, safe preprocessing rules, a Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), and two exact approaches: one is based on Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) approach, and the second represents a novel Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC) approach. These two exact approaches are compared to ILP--alongside GRASP and the Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) from literature. Experiments on 250 random graphs with up to 500 vertices reveal complementary strengths: ILP yields the best feasible solutions, LBBD provides the strongest lower bounds and smallest mean optimality gap, and BBC certifies optimality most frequently. We further introduce an NLP application distinguishing human- and AI-generated texts through vocabulary-based graph features. On 42 instances, BBC achieves the smallest mean optimality gap, certifying 16 optima, while GRASP outperforms VNS. Structural analysis of optimal vocabulary separators identifies 113 mandatory and 151 replaceable features across 272 tests, highlighting substantial variability among optimal solutions. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of complementary optimization strategies and the interpretability of optimal vocabulary-based discrimination.

items.title: Optimized CNN Model for Real-World Plant Disease Detection
items.abstract: Agriculture is indispensable for the security of the global food supply; however, diseases that are often unnoticed in their initial stages cause a considerable decline in crop yield. Manual disease detection via traditional means is slow, requires a lot of manpower, and can result in mistakes; thus, it is not appropriate for extensive or instantaneous diagnoses. This study proposes a refined Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model tailored for reliable and automatic detection of plant diseases using images of leaves taken in the field under real-world agricultural conditions. A deep CNN that has been trained on a vast plant disease dataset shows impressive multi-class classification accuracy and at the same time, has low computational demands. Through a mobile or web interface, users can receive feedback that is nearly real-time; thus, it is affordable for farmers who use devices with low resources. The integration of artificial intelligence into the agricultural workflow has made the proposed methodology a scalable, cost-effective, and eco-friendly solution for the prompt detection of diseases and better crop management in the future.

items.title: Optogenetics in neurobiology and neurodegenerative disorders: from neural circuit mechanisms to precision neuromodulation
items.abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis and stroke, are characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment and neural circuit degeneration, leading to severe cognitive and motor deficits. Although considerable progress has been made in understanding their molecular pathology, the circuit level mechanisms driving disease onset and progression remain incompletely understood. Optogenetics, which combines microbial opsins, genetic engineering and optical stimulation, enables reversible, cell-specific control of neuronal activity with millisecond precision and has transformed neuroscience from observational analysis to causal investigation of neural circuits. This review summarizes recent advances in the molecular basis of optogenetics, microbial opsins, gene delivery strategies and optical stimulation technologies, together with their applications in basic neurobiology and neurodegenerative disease research. We discuss how optogenetics has advanced understanding of neural circuit organization, synaptic plasticity, memory, neurodevelopment, sleep regulation, protein aggregation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress and regulated cell death. Although these studies have generated important mechanistic insights and demonstrated functional improvements in experimental models, translation into human therapies remains investigational due to challenges associated with gene delivery, long-term opsin expression, immune compatibility and optical accessibility. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including closed-loop neuromodulation, wireless photostimulation, artificial intelligence-assisted neural decoding, nanotechnology enabled light delivery and brain computer interfaces, are critically evaluated with emphasis on their current evidence status, translational challenges and limitations for clinical implementation. Collectively, optogenetics provides an unprecedented platform for deciphering disease mechanisms and evaluating circuit-based neuromodulation strategies, while continued technological and biological validation will determine its future role in precision therapies for neurodegenerative disorders.

items.title: Organizations in Interaction With Stakeholders and the Environment
items.abstract: Organizations operate in complex environments shaped by stakeholders, institutions, regulations, technologies and societal expectations. Their ability to survive, adapt and create value depends not only on internal capabilities but also on their responses to external pressures and on maintaining legitimacy. Relationships among organizations, stakeholders and organizational environments shape organizational priorities, resource access and opportunities for action. Stakeholder theory, legitimacy and institutional perspectives offer important lenses for understanding how organizations gain support, secure resources and maintain their licence to operate. Governments, customers, employees, investors, communities and advocacy groups all influence organizational choices, often in different and competing ways. Broader environmental forces, including digitalization, artificial intelligence, sustainability challenges, globalization and regulatory change, create both opportunities and constraints. These developments generate new expectations, strategic dilemmas and pressures to adapt. Organizations are embedded within social, economic, political, technological and ecological systems, making context central to organizational analysis and practice.

items.title: Originality as texture
items.abstract: Conventional notions of originality position university students as the sole authors of the work they submit for assessment. This means that originality is seen as a kind of academic alchemy, whereby students draw from other sources to complete their work but must somehow transform it into something that is wholly of themselves. In this chapter, we propose an alternative framing of originality—as a texture of contributions—to acknowledge the interwoven nature of how students produce work with artificial intelligence (AI). The key distinction is that students’ interactions with AI (or others) are understood as textural rather than absolute. In contrast to approaches which attempt to fully disentangle human and AI, this perspective reorients assessment design to consider two different foci for assurance: work and working . Most current assessment focuses on fixed outputs (work), whether interim or final, to assure achievement. However, this approach cannot assure students’ ways of working, which we argue requires assessors to be participants in the dynamic activity involved in generating work. By being participants in working, assessors can more fully understand the nature of students’ contributions to the work they submit for assessment, and so can make further assurances about the originality of that work.

items.title: Out of sync: Accommodation, evaluation, and emergence in five weeks with an agentic AI teammate
items.abstract: As agentic AI in education shifts from reactive tools toward partners that take initiative and persist over time, a central question is how learners relate to, evaluate, and benefit from artificial agency. We conducted a longitudinal experiment in an undergraduate learning analytics course, in which 17 student teams (N = 48) collaborated with a persistent LLM-based teammate across weekly sessions. The agent decided when to intervene through a trigger-based architecture, and its social role was manipulated between teams: a Cognitive Agent that challenged quick consensus or a Supportive Agent that invited quieter members to contribute. Combining chat discourse, post-session surveys, and spoken reflections, we identified distinct patterns unfolding across three timescales. Students accommodated their language to the agent's role immediately, using more social language toward the Supportive Agent from the first session. Their helpfulness evaluations were recalibrated from session to session in relation to the agent's observed behavior, rather than remaining anchored to students' pre-existing attitudes toward AI. A slower crossover emerged in perceived collaboration process and positive-affect word use in reflections: Supportive-Agent teams began below Cognitive-Agent teams and ended above them, although students rated the Supportive Agent less helpful throughout. Because these responses follow different trajectories, single-session evaluations of agentic AI may miss changes that emerge only through repeated interaction.

items.title: P-ContextBench: From Personal Fact Recall to Personalized Agent Behavior
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for personal tasks, yet evaluating their safe use of personal context remains difficult because such contexts are private, fragmented, dynamic, and socially situated. We introduce P-ContextBench, a realistic, verifiable, and scalable benchmark for evaluating personal-context understanding. P-ContextBench constructs population-structured, life-story-grounded digital humans from demographic seeds reflecting the U.S. population. Rather than using explicit, static profiles, P-ContextBench embeds traits, routines, goals, and constraints as implicit evidence across fragmented, evolving synthetic mobile-app records. It evaluates five capabilities: single-source fact recovery, multi-source fact recovery, temporal state tracking, inference of higher-level personal patterns from routine behavior, and safe handling of requests conflicting with persona-specific constraints through compliance, warning, clarification, or refusal. A multi-stage validation pipeline checks persona plausibility, context recoverability, information leakage, evidence preservation, test-case grounding, and human-judge agreement. We instantiate P-ContextBench with 100 personas, 10,088 hidden facts, 18,261 app-trace fragments, and 4,810 verified test cases. The pipeline supports configurable generation across scales and demographic groups. Cost-effective state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs relevant to personal agents achieve below 60% accuracy on temporal tracking, higher-level pattern inference, and constraint-aware action-boundary decisions, with fewer than 10% of test cases answered correctly across all three repeated runs. Even a high-performing SOTA model remains inconsistent on these capabilities. P-ContextBench provides measurable targets for improving the accuracy, reliability, and safety of LLM-based personal agents.

items.title: Paradigm Shifts in Interstate Conflict? The Strategic Effects of AI and Space-Based Military Technologies
items.abstract: This paper examines whether recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and space-based military technologies have produced a paradigm shift in interstate conflict or have primarily enhanced the conduct of warfare within an existing strategic framework.Existing research has largely emphasized technological development and operational efficiency, while paying comparatively less attention to whether military innovation fundamentally transforms the strategic logic through which battlefield success is converted into strategic outcomes.To address this gap, the paper develops an analytical framework combining the concepts of paradigm shift, critical juncture, and military innovation.It distinguishes tactical and operational change from strategic transformation and argues that a paradigm shift occurs only when technological innovation becomes sufficiently institutionalized to generate a durable transformation in how wars are fought, won, and terminated.Using a qualitative comparative design, the study contrasts short-term decisive operations with prolonged conflicts and evaluates the effects of AI-enabled and space-based systems across both operational and strategic criteria.The findings show that these technologies substantially enhance surveillance, target identification, precision strike, command coordination, and battlespace awareness when objectives are limited and targets are identifiable in advance.Their strategic effects, however, diminish as conflicts become prolonged, when geography, manpower, industrial capacity, political resilience, and escalation management reassert their importance.It therefore argues that recent military innovation has produced substantial tactical and operational transformation without yet displacing the underlying strategic grammar of warfare.It academically contributes by providing a clearer analytical threshold for distinguishing military innovation from a genuine paradigm shift, while acknowledging that the recent and ongoing nature of the cases and reliance on publicly available qualitative evidence limit definitive conclusions about their longer-term strategic consequences.

items.title: Participant-Specific Adaptive Label Smoothing Using Subjective Workload Responses for Cognitive Workload Classification from EEG
items.abstract: Background: Cognitive workload classification from electroencephalography is affected by interindividual variability in EEG signals and subjective workload responses. We propose participant-specific adaptive label smoothing, in which the change in perceived workload between resting and task conditions controls the target confidence, while the experimental class remains unchanged. Methods: The method was evaluated on the STEW dataset and compared with five alternative supervision strategies. Two classification models were used: a feature-based convolutional neural network and a multi-scale Swin Transformer network (MST-Net) operating on time-frequency representations. Global and participant-specific stratified normalization were evaluated using participant-disjoint cross-validation. The participant-specific approach used normalization statistics estimated from each unseen participant’s own unlabeled EEG data. Results: Under stratified normalization, adaptive label smoothing produced the highest macro F1 for both models, with values of 0.768 and 0.796, and ROC AUC values of 0.844 and 0.878, respectively. It also maintained high recall for both classes. Conclusions: The findings suggest that participant-specific subjective workload responses can be used to modulate target confidence, with the most consistent benefit observed under participant-specific normalization. As the strategies differ in target definitions and no hard rest/task or fixed label-smoothing control was evaluated, the differences are descriptive.

items.title: PathCowork: Learning from real-world pathology practice to build AI copilots
items.abstract: Medical AI learns from the answers doctors record, but rarely from how they interpret the evidence to reach them. Here we introduce PathCowork, a framework that turns pathologists' narrated examinations into supervision for visual grounding and procedures that guide diagnostic AI agents. Synchronized gaze, narration and navigation link visual findings to the process of interpreting them. Across 48 sessions from 16 pathologists, the platform captured 1,028 minutes of slide review. Using these data, we trained PathCowork-1T for server deployment and PathCowork-27B for local deployment, with improved visual grounding. Across five organ-specific evaluations, agents combining this grounding with recorded diagnostic procedures achieved primary task scores averaging 17.9 and 24.1 percentage points higher than Claude Code and Codex, respectively, with shorter processing times and lower inference costs. Compared to the state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning AIs, the PathCowork agent-proposed regions achieved higher prostate-grading scores with limited slide labels. PathCowork can also help construct pathology AI benchmarks where questions derived from the recordings identified difficulties in recognizing viewing context and rejecting inapplicable premises. In summary, PathCowork proposes a new paradigm to scale up the data collection and train pathology AI through transparent reasoning from diagnostic sessions, opening a path towards systems that learn directly from routine clinical practice.

items.title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
items.abstract: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

items.title: Pediatrician attitudes, acceptance, and concerns regarding artificial intelligence in pediatric care: a web-based survey in Türkiye
items.abstract: In Türkiye, pediatricians’ perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI), including their knowledge, trust, and concerns, remain underexplored. This study aims to evaluate pediatricians’ knowledge, perceptions, and acceptance of AI in pediatric care. A cross-sectional, open, web-based convenience survey was conducted among pediatricians in Türkiye, including residents and specialists. The survey assessed their knowledge of AI, perceptions of its benefits and risks, and acceptance of AI as a clinical decision support tool. A total of 403 pediatricians accessed the survey; 18 declined to participate, 1 was excluded for a completion time under two minutes, and 16 were excluded for an inconsistent control-item. After excluding responses, 368 were included in the analysis. Participants had a median age of 35 years and a median of 9 years of pediatric care experience. Only 9.5% of participants reported awareness of AI in pediatrics, and 85.9% rated their self-perceived AI knowledge as average or below. Despite this, 74.2% agreed that AI will improve pediatrics, and 88.3% stated it could enhance care quality. Concerns included legal liability (78.5%), data security (54.6%), and the black-box nature of AI (59.2%). Across all 37 ordinal items, a single age correlation survived: younger respondents were more likely to expect AI to increase diagnostic confidence (r s = -0.171, 95% CI -0.269 to -0.070, small effect size; P = 0.001; P adj = 0.038). While 90.8% supported AI as a clinical decision support tool, only 17.4% believed AI could replace human physicians in non-invasive roles. Only 19.3% expected their institution to allocate financial or personnel resources for AI integration. Survey respondents generally view AI as a promising tool to improve pediatric care but express significant concerns about its reliability, ethical implications, and legal responsibilities.

items.abstract: This study aims to analyze student engagement in learning whole numbers up to 10,000 using the Magic Pocket media among fourth-grade students at SDN Jombor 3 Sukoharjo. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed in this research. The subjects consisted of 8 students (2 male and 6 female students) with diverse cognitive ability backgrounds. Data collection techniques included structured observation, semi-structured interviews, performance documentation, and diagnostic tests. The data were analyzed using data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The results indicate that the Magic Pocket media significantly increased active student engagement across three primary dimensions: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Students with lower initial abilities demonstrated high enthusiasm and an improved conceptual understanding of place value through visual and hands-on manipulation. Female students showed high precision in place value organization, whereas male students performed strongly in interactive speed and problem-solving activities. Overall, the Magic Pocket media proved to be an effective concrete instructional tool for enhancing student engagement in elementary mathematics learning.

items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence in education opens up opportunities to support learning while also raising ethical issues related to academic integrity and students’ digital responsibility. This article aims to analyze the role of character education as a foundation for guiding the use of artificial intelligence in relation to these two aspects. The study employs a literature review using a descriptive-qualitative approach. The findings indicate that the values of ṣidq and amanah provide a conceptual foundation for transparency in AI use, recognition of intellectual contributions, adherence to assignment guidelines, and accountability for learning processes and outcomes. Meanwhile, the values of tabayyun, respect for others, and a focus on the common good underpin digital responsibility in the form of information verification, privacy protection, respect for intellectual property, and consideration of the social impacts of AI use. Strengthening these two aspects requires educators to lead by example, clear institutional guidelines, family support, and reflective learning grounded in ethical dilemmas. This article concludes that the integration of character education and AI literacy should be directed toward developing students who are proficient in using technology while also being able to make decisions honestly and responsibly. The resulting conceptual framework still requires empirical testing according to educational levels and contexts.

items.title: Penguatan Kompetensi Guru dalam Mengembangkan Media Pembelajaran Interaktif Menggunakan Canva AI
items.abstract: Teachers' competence in designing technology-based interactive learning media is one of the key factors for successful 21st-century learning. However, initial mapping at SMP Plus Aisyah Samawa revealed that approximately 70% of teachers still relied on conventional learning media, and more than 80% were unfamiliar with the Artificial Intelligence (AI) features of the Canva design platform, such as Magic Design, AI Presentation, and Text to Image. This community service program aimed to strengthen teachers' technical and pedagogical competence in developing interactive learning media using Canva AI, integrated with lesson plans (RPP) or teaching modules. The program was implemented in three stages: preparation, implementation (socialization, hands-on training with a 30% theory–70% practice composition, and classroom technology application), and evaluation, supported by three months of intensive post-training mentoring. Program success indicators were measured through pretest–posttest score improvements, the percentage of teachers producing interactive learning media products, and the integration of such media into lesson plans or teaching modules. The results showed an improvement in teachers' competence in utilizing Canva's AI features and an increase in student engagement during the learning process. This program is expected to serve as a replicable model for strengthening teachers' digital literacy in other pesantren-based schools in Sumbawa Regency, while contributing to the achievement of SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure).

items.abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to design and develop furniture as a medium or assistive tool to foster children’s disciplined behavior in returning their belongings to designated places at home. Methodology: The study employed an ergonomic product design approach integrated with a biomimicry design method. Findings: The study produced a piece of furniture whose form and colors resemble the fruit of the Patuk Manuk plant (Thunbergia alata). Observations indicated that the product created an enjoyable experience for children when placing their belongings neatly and systematically. The System Usability Scale (SUS) yielded a score of 80, indicating good usability, while the Godspeed questionnaire demonstrated high reliability, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.93. Conclusion: The study developed an ergonomic assistive product that supports the development of disciplined behavior in children. The product demonstrated good usability, was well accepted by both children and parents, and provided an enjoyable experience for users interacting with it. Originality: The design integrates ergonomic product design and biomimicry, a combination that remains relatively uncommon in innovative product development. Integrating these approaches is expected to provide complementary benefits in developing learning aids that support the formation of disciplined habits among children in the home environment.

items.title: Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence, Naturalistic Decision-Making and Cognitive Flexibility: A Systematic Literature Review and an Integrated Mediation Model
items.abstract: This study systematically reviews the literature on the relationships between individuals' perceptions of artificial intelligence, naturalistic decision-making and cognitive flexibility, and synthesizes the evidence into an integrated model in which cognitive flexibility mediates the effect of artificial intelligence perceptions on naturalistic decision-making. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, three Boolean searches corresponding to the pairwise relationships were run in OpenAlex on 20 October 2026 and complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Of 1,161 records identified, 1,140 were screened, 99 were assessed in full and 70 met the eligibility criteria; together with 32 studies reached through citation tracking, 102 studies were coded and synthesized thematically. The synthesis shows that the three constructs have been studied in largely separate streams: research on artificial intelligence and decision-making concentrates on advice-taking, reliance and decision-making styles; research on artificial intelligence and cognitive flexibility is very recent, concentrated in educational and health settings and consistent in sign; and research on cognitive flexibility and decision-making draws on laboratory, neurophysiological and survey evidence. Cognitive flexibility is a replicated mediator in adjacent domains, but no study has tested the full chain from artificial intelligence perceptions through cognitive flexibility to naturalistic decision-making. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Flexibility Theory and the recognition-primed decision model, the study formulates four testable propositions, presents an integrated model, identifies measurement options and outlines a research agenda.

items.title: PhysCount: Do MLLMs Count Visual Appearances or Physical Entities?
items.abstract: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.

items.title: Pilot Assessments of Terminal-Area Logic and Equipage-Specific Symbols While Using the Airborne Collision Avoidance System Xr During Uncrewed Operations
items.abstract: Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS) operations are expected to increase traffic complexity in terminal-area airspace, creating new challenges for tactical separation assurance and pilot decision-making. This study evaluated subjective pilot responses to the latest version of the Airborne Collision Avoidance System for rotorcraft (ACAS Xr) during simulated RPAS operations in approach, departure, and en-route conditions. Eleven IFR-rated fixed-wing pilots completed simulated flight scenarios using ACAS Xr, including encounters involving cooperative and non-cooperative traffic and dynamic terminal-area logic. Subjective measures were collected and included workload, usability, and operational acceptability. Pilots rated ACAS Xr positively for guidance effectiveness, safe separation support, and traffic-symbol clarity for aircraft equipped and not equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast. However, terminal-area warning alerts were sometimes perceived as untimely or operationally inappropriate, particularly Level Off and Descend advisories. Results support continued development of ACAS Xr while highlighting areas requiring refinement for terminal-area operations.

items.title: Precision Medicine Using Artificial Intelligence and Genomics: A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Precision medicine is an emerging healthcare paradigm that tailors prevention, diagnosis, and treatment to individual patients using genetic, clinical, environmental, and lifestyle information. Advances in next-generation sequencing, bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) now allow clinicians to analyse genomic variants, stratify disease risk, and select therapies at a level of individual detail that population-averaged medicine cannot provide. This paper reviews AI-enabled precision medicine, synthesising landmark and recent peer-reviewed literature published between 2004 and 2026, and tracing the field from early blood-group stratification through the Human Genome Project to national precision medicine programmes and the multimodal AI of the present day. A conceptual framework is proposed that integrates electronic health records, genomic sequencing, laboratory tests, and wearable-device data in a secure platform where AI models identify biomarkers, predict risk, and recommend treatment for clinician validation; it is synthesised from literature-reported practices rather than experimentally validated. Applications in oncology, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, rare genetic disorders, pharmacogenomics, and remote monitoring are examined, followed by the main challenges, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, unrepresentative genomic datasets, cost, interpretability, and ethics, together with mitigation strategies. Emerging directions, including digital twins, federated learning, multimodal AI, and CRISPR-assisted therapies, are discussed. This review highlights the role of AI and genomics in moving healthcare from reactive to predictive and personalised, and identifies priorities for future research.

items.title: Predictive modeling and multi-objective optimization of 3D-printed PLA parts using a hybrid random vector functional link (RVFL) and henry gas solubility optimization (HGSO) framework
items.abstract: To forecast the mechanical characteristics of 3D printed Polylactic Acid (PLA) specimens, this work explores artificial intelligence models. Tensile strength (TS) and surface roughness (Ra) of printed parts were examined in relation to five process parameters: build angle (BA), infill angle (IA), layer thickness (LT), printing speed (PS), and nozzle temperature (NT). In the machine learning modelling stage models such as Random Vector Functional Link (RVFL), Random Vector Functional Link tuned by Henry Gas Solubility Optimization (RVFL-HGSO), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) were created to forecast the printed parts’ surface roughness and tensile strength. Moreover this study shows the effectiveness of random vector functional link model tuned by the Henry Gas Solubility Optimization (RVFL-HGSO) when predicting surface roughness. The developed model achieved highest R2 = 98.95%, RMSE = 0.777, MAPE = 1.002%, and MAE = 0.514 on test dataset. It increased R2 by 4.98% when compared with RVFL and by 9.93% when compared with ANN on test dataset. RVFL-HGSO decreased MAPE by 49.93%, also MAE by 53.90%, and RMSE by 29.68% when compared with RVFL on test dataset. It also, decreased MAPE by 69.02%, also MAE by 73.95%, and RMSE by 58.49% when compared with ANN. The multi-objective optimization by particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) gives best possible solution at place of BA = 44.16, NT = 220, IA = 14.93, LT = 0.22, PS = 45.18: Minimum predicted Ra = 2.53 and maximum predicted TS = 44.15. The findings demonstrate the RVFL-HGSO model’s unique method for finding intricate correlations in the dataset, laying the groundwork for better product design and mechanical property optimization through process parameter adjustment.

items.title: Predictors of Lower Back Musculoskeletal Disability Among Emergency Department Healthcare Professionals: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs), particularly lower back (LB) pain are highly prevalent in emergency department (ED) healthcare professionals with significant health-related impacts due to the high and unexpected workload. Objective: This study aimed to identify the predictors of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals in Jordan, including physical, psychological, and ergonomic occupational factors. Methods: A multicenter convenience sample of ED healthcare professionals was recruited from Jordanian ED departments. Data collection included demographics, ergonomics-related factors and a group of validated outcome measures: the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21). A stepwise multivariable linear regression model was used to identify predictors of LB disability. Results: The study included 447 participants, of whom 57% were male ( n = 255) and had a mean age of 35.1 ± 7.0 years. Predictors of the ODI ( R 2 = .31) included depression ( B = 0.456, p < .001), taking sick leave in the past 12 months (β = 6.8, p < .001), safe handling and posturing practices ( B = −5.584, p < .001), age ( B = 0.32, p < .001) and presence of musculoskeletal injury in the past 12 months ( B = 4.6, p = .022). Conclusion: This study highlights the burden of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals. LB disability was significantly associated with depression, recent Musculoskeletal injury, Musculoskeletal-related sick leave and older age, with safe handling and posture practices showing a protective effect. items.title: Preparation and Outlook for the Era of Solo Entrepreneurship: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework for Artificial Intelligence Service–Centered Startups
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) now enables individuals to develop and operate services that formerly required the resources of entire organizations, creating a distinct wave of solo entrepreneurship centered on AI services.This study defines AI-based solo entrepreneurship as venture creation in which one founder, without cofounders or employees, designs, builds, and operates a market offering by embedding AI tools as core productive capacity rather than peripheral aids.It analyzes how this transformation unfolds and identifies the capabilities and challenges founders must prepare for.Drawing on an integrative review of domestic and international literature and a structured, criteria-based analysis of documented AI-based solo-venture cases, the study distinguishes success determinants from the barriers founders commonly encounter.The analysis identifies three capabilities most associated with success-proficiency with AI tools, digital marketing capability, and a disposition toward continuous learning-and recurrent barriers of psychological resistance to technology, funding difficulty, weak marketing and sales capability, and isolation and burnout from working alone.Building on these findings, the study proposes an integrated analytical model that cross-examines success factors and barriers across four dimensions-capability, resources, market, and psychology-and derives a four-stage strategy (preparation, execution, growth, and scale-up) with policy tasks in education, institutions, and finance.Because the model is conceptually derived rather than empirically validated, it is advanced as a set of testable propositions rather than confirmed results.This study contributes by specifying concretely the preparations required of individuals, firms, and government and situating its integrated model against established entrepreneurship frameworks to assess its distinct contribution.

items.title: Preparing Modernisation Decisions of Public IT Recruitment through a Semi-Automated NLP Approach to Mapping Gov-ernmental Syllabi onto ESCO and e-CF
items.abstract: The rapid digitalisation of public services and the emergence of artificial intelligence, data science, and cybersecurity have exposed limitations in existing competency frameworks for public-sector IT professionals. In Spain, the long-standing examination syllabus for Level A IT civil servants is undergoing reform to address the growing misalignment between assessed competencies and current professional requirements. This paper presents a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop process to support decision-making by mapping the existing syllabus and authoritative European professional profiles to two complementary frameworks: the European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations (ESCO) taxonomy and the European e-Competence Framework (e-CF, EN 16234-1). The pipeline uses Sentence-BERT (S-BERT) with MPNet-based embeddings and cosine similarity to identify relevant skills and competences. Before automated matching, specialised profiles in artificial intelligence, data science, and cybersecurity, including references published by the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), are harmonised using consistent ESCO and e-CF terminology. The resulting candidate profiles are ranked for stakeholder consideration and consolidated through expert validation. By combining semantic matching, multi-source harmonisation, and expert judgement, the proposed approach reduces complex information to a manageable set of profiles, supporting decisions on candidate selection and competency development in public-sector IT. The methodology provides a replicable approach for modernising public recruitment in alignment with European competency frameworks.

items.title: Preservice Teachers' Perceptions of Digital Platforms: Insights into Moodle and AI Apps for Lesson Planning and Delivery
items.abstract: Preservice teachers are increasingly integrating technologies such as Moodle and AI-driven (artificial intelligence) applications into their pedagogical preparation; however, their attitudes toward these tools remain underexplored. The study examined preservice teachers' perceptions of digital platforms: insights into Moodle and AI apps for lesson planning and delivery. The study adopts the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as its theoretical framework. A qualitative research approach was employed, utilising an interpretive phenomenological design to examine preservice teachers' lived experiences and attitudes in depth. The population comprised 243 preservice teachers enrolled in a Bachelor of Education program at a South African university. A purposive sample of 12 participants was selected, ensuring representation across year levels and subject specialisations based on their exposure to digital platforms. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews. Data analysis followed Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis process, using NVivo software, which involved familiarisation, code generation, theme development, and review for rigour. The study findings revealed that preservice teachers described Moodle as highly useful for collaborative lesson planning, praising its resource-sharing features for fostering peer feedback and organisation in group projects. The study concluded that preservice teachers hold largely favourable attitudes toward digital platforms, affirming their role in competency development. However, there are still gaps in AI familiarity, highlighting the need for teacher training. These attitudes align with TAM predictions, understanding the need for intentional integration. The study recommends embedding Moodle and AI modules in preservice curricula and providing hands-on workshops to boost confidence and address barriers.

items.title: Prevalence of and factors associated with work-related musculoskeletal disorders among orthopedic nurses: a cross-sectional study with exploratory interpretable machine-learning modeling
items.abstract: Objective This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of musculoskeletal symptoms and work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) among orthopedic nurses, identify demographic, occupational, and lifestyle characteristics associated with WMSDs, and explore whether routinely collected characteristics could discriminate nurses with WMSDs from those without. Method A single-center cross-sectional study was conducted among nurses at a tertiary orthopedic specialty hospital in China between March and November 2023. Conventional analyses included multivariable logistic regression, modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors, and negative binomial regression. Logistic regression as a benchmark, elastic-net logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and support vector machine were compared using repeated 5-fold cross-validation with fold-specific preprocessing. Prediction performance was assessed using AUC with bootstrap 95% CIs, PR-AUC, Brier score, calibration intercept and slope, and descriptive threshold metrics; TreeSHAP was used for model interpretation. Result Among 948 nurses with valid questionnaires, 654 reported musculoskeletal symptoms in the previous 12 months, irrespective of work attribution (68.99%). After excluding 44 participants with uncertain work-related attribution, 604/904 participants were classified as having work-related WMSDs (66.81%). Each 1-point increase in the strict ergonomic risk score was associated with WMSDs in logistic regression (adjusted OR = 2.631, 95% CI 2.039–3.432; p < 0.001) and modified Poisson regression (adjusted PR = 1.283, 95% CI 1.203–1.369; p < 0.001). The highest observed AUC was 0.752 (95% CI 0.721–0.791) for the domain random forest model; the domain XGBoost model had the highest PR-AUC (0.841). Conclusion Musculoskeletal symptoms and WMSDs were common among orthopedic nurses in this single-center sample. Occupational exposure and postural load were associated with WMSDs. The exploratory prediction models showed limited-to-moderate discrimination and warrant prospective multicenter external validation before practical application.

items.title: Prevalence of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Symptoms in Farmers Operating Motorized Equipment
items.abstract: Background: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy of the upper limb, resulting from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel.Occupational risk factors include repetitive wrist movements, forceful hand exertion, hand-arm vibration, and non-neutral wrist postures.Farmers operating motorized agricultural equipment may be exposed to these occupational stresses; however, evidence regarding questionnaire-reported CTS symptoms among Indian farmers remains limited.Objective: This study aimed to estimate the proportion of farmers reporting symptoms suggestive of CTS while operating motorized agricultural equipment and to examine the association between symptom severity and functional status using the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCTQ), supplemented by clinical examination.Methods: A cross-sectional observational study was conducted among 90 farmers aged 25-45 years operating motorized agricultural equipment in and around Karad, Maharashtra, India.Participants were recruited through convenience sampling based on predefined eligibility criteria.The BCTQ was used as the primary patient-reported outcome measure and included the 11-item Symptom Severity Scale (SSS) and the eightitem Functional Status Scale (FSS).Responses were categorized into five levels: no symptoms or difficulty, mild, moderate, severe, and very severe.Phalen's test, Tinel's sign, and the Durkan compression test were also performed.Spearman's rank correlation was used to assess the association between participant-level BCTQ total scores.Results: Of the 90 participants, 74 (82.22%) were male and 16 (17.78%)were female.Among the 90 participants, 19 (21.11%) reported symptoms suggestive of CTS.The 95% confidence interval (CI) was 14.0-30.6%.Mild, moderate, and severe symptoms were present in three (3.33%),eight (8.89%), and eight (8.89%) participants, respectively.Mild, moderate, and severe functional difficulty occurred in three (3.33%),11 (12.22%), and five (5.56%) participants, respectively.Participant-level BCTQ total scores showed a very strong positive Spearman correlation (r = 0.9747, p = 0.0167).Conclusion: In this cross-sectional study, 19 of 90 farmers (21.11%) reported symptoms suggestive of CTS.This finding represents questionnaire-reported symptoms in a convenience sample and should not be interpreted as the prevalence of confirmed CTS.Greater reported symptom severity coincided with greater reported functional difficulty; however, this relationship should be interpreted cautiously because both outcomes were assessed using related components of the BCTQ.The study does not establish that operating motorized agricultural equipment causes CTS symptoms, nor does it demonstrate the effectiveness of screening or ergonomic interventions.Further studies involving larger and more representative samples, detailed occupational exposure assessment, evaluation of relevant confounding factors, and objective diagnostic methods such as nerve conduction studies (NCSs) are warranted.Such research may help guide evidence-based occupational screening and preventive strategies for agricultural workers.

items.title: Privacy, AI, and Social Media Platforms
items.abstract: The right to privacy in Africa remains underdeveloped within the African Union legal framework, with the Banjul Charter containing no explicit privacy provision. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence has fundamentally transformed privacy dynamics through social media platforms’ unprecedented data collection. This chapter examines the normative status of privacy in Africa and identifies pathways for strengthening protection against AI-driven violations. It first documents how AI’s dependency on data, coupled with surveillance capitalism’s business models, creates novel threats: platforms exploit the ‘privacy paradox’ (the gap between users’ expressed concerns and their actual data-sharing behaviour) to collect vast quantities of personal information, with African users particularly vulnerable given limited privacy literacy. It then assesses the regulatory framework: international human rights law recognises privacy as fundamental, but the Banjul Charter’s silence creates a normative gap that fragmented national data protection laws cannot fill. The Malabo Convention represents significant progress, though questions remain regarding the distinction between privacy and data protection. Finally, the chapter explores interpretive and regulatory pathways to strengthen privacy protection against AI-driven threats while maintaining coherence with regional human rights obligations.

items.title: PrivacyFlow: Privacy in AI Agents through Information Flow Analysis and Consequence-Aware Risk Management
items.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents executing multi-step workflows over personal data often misalign with user privacy expectations and leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Although Contextual Integrity (CI) formalizes this problem, existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalize CI for realistic multi-step task sequences in evolving environments. In this work, we first introduce agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets for sensitive information. We also introduce PrivacyFlow, a defense that separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1), treating each sharing decision as a structured risk-management problem. Before execution, PrivacyFlow traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. This allows us to model the downstream consequences of disclosure, including inference attacks and context-dependent harms. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or consults the user. Across six models, PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22--55 percentage points. We further highlight a new privacy--utility--autonomy tradeoff: allowing PrivacyFlow to proactively prompt the user in case of uncertainty can increase authorized task completion at the cost of shifting decision effort back to the user. Our results suggest that proactive CI reasoning can substantially improve agentic privacy and motivate further study of this tradeoff.

items.title: PrivateAgent: Mobility-Aware AI Agents for Safe Private Networks
items.abstract: Abstract Private cellular networks increasingly support video analytics, connected workers, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and other industrial applications whose mobility and control deadlines vary widely. A single artificial-intelligence (AI) agent cannot safely manage all of these loops because perception, planning, networking, and governance operate at different time scales and execution locations. This paper presents PrivateAgent, a mobility-aware framework that classifies private-network applications as stationary, low-mobility, or high-mobility and maps their functions across device, site-edge, and cloud tiers. Hard real-time perception and actuation remain local; near-real-time planning and network optimization run at the edge; long-horizon learning runs in the cloud. Network-changing actions are represented as typed artifacts with explicit evidence, scope, authority, monitoring, and rollback requirements before execution. We detail representative use cases including perimeter video, machine vision, connected workers, forklifts, AMRs, and drones, and specify suitable agent families, latency targets, failure modes, and benchmark dimensions. We also instantiate the action-admission boundary with SafeFlow-Real50, a 50-scenario benchmark derived from four anonymized private-network traces. In a blind evaluation, the model selected the correct act/clarify/reject mode in 50/50 scenarios, an acceptable action in 45/50, and the preferred action in 43/50. The deterministic gateway detected all 400 injected corruptions versus 150 for schema-only validation. These results show that mobility should determine the real-time agent boundary, while independent validation should determine whether generated network actions may advance toward execution.

items.title: Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models
items.abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.

items.title: Productive Friction and Learner Engagement in Genai Supported EFL Vocabulary Learning
items.abstract: This article explains how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) prompts can support durable vocabulary learning while preserving learner engagement and autonomy in English as a foreign language (EFL) education. A purposive conceptual synthesis integrates vocabulary research, retrieval practice, task involvement, cognitive load, self regulation, and AI literacy. The analysis distinguishes established findings from proposed relationships and develops the AI Mediated Cognitive Engagement Model (ACEM). ACEM locates potential learning benefits in the sequencing of an initial attempt, contingent assistance, evaluative feedback, contextual reuse, and later retrieval. Productive friction is defined prospectively through learning relevant demands, accessible support, and opportunities for error repair; its effectiveness requires independent testing. Four propositions address retrieval, proficiency dependent support, evaluative reuse, and learner control. The synthesis is selective and reports no intervention data. The proposed mechanisms require comparisons that separate prompt sequence effects from exposure, time, feedback quality, and technological novelty. Teachers can use a graduated prompt sequence, verified lexical resources, and equivalent offline tasks to protect participation, reduce unnecessary interface demands, and assess learning after AI assistance is withdrawn. The framework connects prompt design with observable learner activity and delayed lexical outcomes, while treating emotional engagement, teacher judgement, and equitable access as conditions of implementation.

items.abstract: The most widespread promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for solo entrepreneurs is time savings. Experimental evidence documents substantial gains on well-defined tasks, but large-scale adoption studies find modest self-reported savings, and at least one randomized trial with experienced professionals found an increase, rather than a reduction, in completion time. This theoretical essay argues that part of this discrepancy stems from conflating gross productivity — the time saved in generating an output — with net productivity — the time and value saved after accounting for task specification, verification, correction, rework, context switching, and the expected cost of errors that escape review. For solo entrepreneurs, this distinction is especially relevant because the same person generates, reviews, corrects, and answers for errors, with no division of labor to absorb these costs. Integrating the economics of productivity and time allocation, the literature on quality costs and rework, research on automation and overreliance, human–AI interaction studies, and recent empirical evidence on GenAI at work, we propose an accounting model of net productivity, with explicit cost components and boundary conditions, and derive eight propositions. We discuss implications for solo entrepreneurs, limitations, and a study design with task-level randomization and an illustrative power calculation. The article presents no empirical data; its propositions are intended for testing.

items.title: Program-wide approaches to changing assessment in response to GenAI
items.abstract: Given the rapid development and increased availability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), adapting assessment so that it builds student GenAI literacy and assures student learning in scalable and sustainable ways is imperative. In this chapter, we discuss different approaches that can be taken to address the need to change assessment in response to GenAI. We also present a case study of one potentially scalable and sustainable way to address this challenge, a program-wide approach adopted to review assessment across three health programs in response to GenAI. Team members received GenAI professional development; all assessment tasks in core units were then mapped, and collaborative discussions undertaken within teams to identify key opportunities within the program to both build student GenAI literacy and minimise the impact of GenAI on assuring learning. Assessment changes were then made. The chapter then outlines the affordances and challenges of this program-wide, collaborative approach to redesigning assessment given the impact of GenAI, and discusses undertaking program-wide assessment change in response to GenAI.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: Programmable Auxetic Metamaterial‐Based E‐Skin for Conformable Dual‐Mechanism Spatiotemporal Sensing
items.abstract: ABSTRACT While self‐powered flexible e‐skins based on nanogenerators hold immense promise for wearable electronics, severe interfacial mechanical mismatches occur under complex joint deformations, limiting reliable multichannel sensing. Herein, a 4D‐printed mechanical metamaterial‐enabled e‐skin with an auxetic scaffold and AI‐assisted decoding is developed to improve deformation accommodation and support multichannel sensing during joint motion. Benefiting from an auxetic architecture with a tunable negative Poisson's ratio (−0.41 to −1.76), the metamaterial skeleton expands laterally under stretch to mimic the strain‐stiffening behavior of biological tissues. By concentrating local stress, this geometrical programmability transforms the skeleton into an active mechanical amplifier, significantly boosting the triboelectric‐piezoelectric (TENG/PENG) responses. An integrated nine‐channel array captures these amplified spatiotemporal features with high fidelity. During fast running, the device yields robust 3 V outputs and resolves 3 Hz rhythmic motions. Further, by introducing a lightweight 1D convolutional neural network (1D‐CNN) to decouple intricate spatiotemporal crosstalk, the system achieves advanced motion‐state classification with an exceptional accuracy of over 95% on average across different tasks. This integration of mechanics and artificial intelligence offers a robust platform for next‐generation intelligent wearable rehabilitation and human‐machine interfaces.

items.title: Prompt engineering as an extension of information literacy: Implications for library instruction programmes
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now a routine information tool for students and knowledge workers, and the quality of what they obtain depends in part on how they instruct it. This article argues that prompt engineering is best understood as an extension of information literacy, and that library and information professionals should lead its teaching in partnership with other units. Using conceptual analysis, it maps prompt competencies onto the six frames of the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education and, unlike earlier mappings, identifies where the analogy fails. The mapping holds for question formulation, evaluation and refinement. It fails where a language model generates text and does not retrieve documents, where its sources cannot be inspected, and where it fabricates citations. Those failures are the strongest argument for librarian involvement, because they call for verification skills that prompt technique alone does not supply. The article proposes an instructional design in four strands, including one for workplace settings, sets out how each can be assessed, and considers equity of access to instruction. It also addresses two objections: that prompt engineering is a transient skill, and that librarians are not yet prepared to teach it. The argument is conceptual and requires empirical evaluation.
